entities.name: Hunminjeongeum (The Correct/Proper Sounds for the Instruction of the People)
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The document promulgated by King Sejong the Great of the Joseon dynasty in 1446 CE, introducing the Korean alphabetical script now known as Hangul. Sejong created the script because Korean could not be adequately written in Chinese characters, and illiteracy among commoners was widespread. The brilliance of Hangul lies in its scientific design: consonant letters mimic the shape of the speech organs (tongue, lips, throat) used to produce them, vowels are based on philosophical principles (heaven, earth, human), and letters are grouped into syllable blocks.

The original Hunminjeongeum document — both the promulgation and its detailed scholarly commentary (Hunminjeongeum Haeryebon) — is inscribed as a UNESCO Memory of the World (1997). Hangul is widely regarded by linguists as one of the most rationally designed writing systems in history.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Hangul's scientific design and widespread adoption led to a significant increase in literacy among commoners in Korea, contributing to the country's rapid economic growth and cultural development. By the 19th century, Hangul had become an essential tool for education and communication.
